Dodgers make Tarik Skubal decision that should worry Brewers before NLCS showdown originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are four victories away from returning to the World Series, and manager Dave Roberts has revealed how his team plans to attack the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
Roberts announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 on Sunday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to pitch Game 2 on Monday. The decision gives Los Angeles two of baseball's most accomplished pitchers to begin a series that features the National League's top two regular-season teams.
The announcement also provides another reminder of the extraordinary pitching depth the Dodgers have assembled. Los Angeles is attempting to win its third consecutive World Series championship, and its starting rotation could become the biggest obstacle standing between Milwaukee and its own championship ambitions.
Tarik Skubal gets another opportunity to set the tone
Skubal will take the mound Sunday at American Family Field after delivering an excellent performance against the Atlanta Braves in the Division Series. The two-time Cy Young Award winner allowed one run on two hits over six innings in Game 1, striking out seven batters while issuing two walks.
Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting Game 2 for the Dodgers in the NLCS against the Brewers, per @ByJackHarris https://t.co/e8wI91D6uF
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 9, 2026
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster August trade, adding another established ace to an already talented pitching staff. His arrival strengthened a rotation that included Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, giving Roberts multiple options capable of controlling a postseason game.
Starting Skubal in Game 1 is an important decision because Milwaukee owns home-field advantage in the series. The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, while the Dodgers reached the 100-win mark. A strong opening performance would allow Los Angeles to immediately put pressure on a team that has been extremely difficult to beat throughout the year.
Skubal's ability to limit baserunners and generate strikeouts could be particularly valuable against a Milwaukee lineup featuring Christian Yelich, Jackson Chourio and William Contreras.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto gives Dodgers another major advantage
Yamamoto will follow Skubal in Game 2 after producing one of the Dodgers' best pitching performances against Atlanta. The right-hander struck out 10 batters over seven innings, allowing only one run on four hits in a victory that helped Los Angeles regain control of the Division Series.
The performance continued an impressive postseason history for Yamamoto, who earned World Series MVP honors in 2025. His ability to deliver deep, efficient outings gives Roberts another dependable option before the series shifts to Dodger Stadium. Milwaukee is expected to rely heavily on its own talented young pitchers, including Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Brewers have demonstrated throughout the season that they can compete with baseball's most talented rosters, but matching Los Angeles on the mound will be a significant challenge.
The Dodgers also have decisions remaining beyond their first two starters. Roberts indicated Friday that the team was considering adding another pitcher to its NLCS roster, a move that would require removing a position player.
Dodgers still have questions despite pitching advantage
One concern involves veteran utility player Miguel Rojas, who left Game 3 against Atlanta because of lower back discomfort. Rojas participated in baseball activities Friday, but Roberts stopped short of confirming his availability for the championship series.
The Dodgers eliminated Atlanta in four games, while Milwaukee also advanced with a four-game victory over San Diego. The teams now meet in the NLCS for the second consecutive postseason, creating another opportunity for the Brewers to challenge the defending champions. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday at 8 p.m. ET, with Game 2 following Monday at 5 p.m. ET.
Los Angeles has plenty of offensive talent, including Shohei Ohtani, but its starting pitching could determine how this series unfolds. By sending Skubal and Yamamoto to the mound in Milwaukee, Roberts is giving the Dodgers an opportunity to establish control before returning home.

Oct 8, 2026, 11:35 AM ET
New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
More Recent News
Oct 8, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays closer Bryan Baker shut the door in his team's 4-3 win over the New York Yankees in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with two strikeouts. Baker was a key part of Tampa Bay's three-game sweep of New York, logging saves in all three games while allowing just one baserunner to reach. The 31-year-old emerged as one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts and 41 saves across 62 1/3 innings (65 games). Heading into the American League Championship Series, Baker's dominance at the end of games gives Tampa Bay a significant advantage if it can get an early lead on its opponents.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Jakob Marsee Having UCL Repair With Internal Brace


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:24 AM ET
Miami Marlins outfielder Jakob Marsee (elbow) will get a UCL repair with an internal brace of his left elbow on Monday, according to Christina De Nicola of MLB.com. The estimated return-to-play timeline for Marsee is around six months. Marsee battled through elbow issues down the stretch in 2026 in his first full season in the majors with Miami. In his first taste of the big leagues in 2025, Marsee hit .292 (61-for-209) with five home runs, 33 RBI, 14 stolen bases, and 28 runs scored in 55 games and 234 plate appearances. In 155 games and 616 plate appearances this year, Marsee slashed .231/.348/.359 with a .706 OPS, 11 home runs, 41 RBI, 23 stolen bases, and 83 runs scored for the Fish. The 25-year-old former sixth-round pick by the San Diego Padres in 2022 from Central Michigan University has a very intriguing power/speed profile as an outfielder in all fantasy leagues, but his availability for Opening Day in 2027 could be in question, depending on how he fares during his rehab after going under the knife early next week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Oct 8, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Milwaukee Brewers outfielder Garrett Mitchell had a big game in his team's 3-1, series-clinching win over the San Diego Padres in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday. At the plate, Mitchell went two-for-four with a triple, an RBI, and a run scored. In the field, Mitchell robbed Padres third baseman Manny Machado of what would have been a game-tying two-run home run in the eighth inning. The 28-year-old Mitchell was finally able to stay mostly healthy in 2026, hitting .262/.354/.416 with 11 home runs, 65 RBI, 74 runs scored, and 14 stolen bases across 531 plate appearances in the regular season. He was productive in the NLDS as well, logging four hits, three runs scored, an RBI, and a stolen base across 15 at-bats.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Hagen Smith Opening Game 4 of ALDS on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Chicago White Sox rookie left-hander Hagen Smith will serve as the opener in Game 4 of the American League Division Series on Thursday at home against the division-rival Cleveland Guardians, according to Scott Merkin of MLB.com. The 23-year-old former fifth overall pick in 2024 from the University of Arkansas made 18 appearances (only one start) in his major-league debut during the 2026 regular season, posting a nice 1.29 ERA (2.35 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP with 41 strikeouts and 16 walks in 28 innings pitched. The talented young southpaw has already thrown 6 1/3 innings in his first experience in the playoffs, too, allowing just one earned run on three hits while walking five and striking out six. He started Game 1 of the ALDS against Cleveland and threw 2 2/3 shutout innings with three walks and four strikeouts in the team's 3-0 victory before allowing a run with two walks and a strikeout in two-thirds of an inning in Wednesday's Game 3 loss. Smith will probably have a short leash as the White Sox try to close out the best-of-five series, with right-hander Erick Fedde potentially piggybacking Smith in Chicago. In three relief appearances against the Guardians during the regular season, Smith allowed two earned runs with six walks and eight strikeouts in 5 2/3 innings pitched.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Scott Merkin
Victor Mesa Jr. Homers in ALDS-Clinching Win


Will Brady




Oct 8, 2026, 11:14 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. was one of the stars of his team's 4-3 win in Game 3 of the American League Division Series over the New York Yankees, hitting a two-run home run off Yankees left-hander Max Fried. Mesa Jr.'s home run was his only hit of the night, but it gave the Rays a 4-2 lead in the sixth inning that they would ultimately never give back. Across 262 plate appearances in the regular season, Mesa Jr. hit .260/.327/.498 with 14 home runs, 34 RBI, 37 runs scored, and nine stolen bases. After starting the year in the minors, the 25-year-old has emerged as an everyday corner outfielder for Tampa Bay and provides another dynamic power/speed bat for the Rays. If Mesa Jr. can get hot, he could help power a deep postseason run.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 10:01 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers closer Edwin Diaz picked up his second save in as many nights on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with a strikeout in his team's 4-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series. Diaz missed most of the 2026 regular season due to elbow and neck injuries. However, he's been dominant since returning from the injured list in mid-September. Diaz allowed just two baserunners while notching nine strikeouts in his final five innings pitched of the regular season, and he's now logged low-stress saves in each of his first two appearances of the playoffs. With Diaz rounding into form, Los Angeles' bullpen looks like a major strength heading into the National League Championship Series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:52 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians left-hander Foster Griffin was dominant in a bulk relief appearance in his team's 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Griffin followed Cleveland opener Daniel Espino and allowed two hits and one earned run while striking out seven across 2 2/3 innings of work. The 31-year-old was used exclusively as a starting pitcher during the regular season, posting a 15-6 record with a 3.60 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, and 158 strikeouts across 172 2/3 innings (31 starts) split between the Guardians and the Washington Nationals. However, Griffin struggled mightily late in the year, pitching to a 5.05 ERA in the second half and a 6.87 ERA across 18 1/3 innings in September. If Griffin can rediscover his early-season form in a bullpen role, he could help Cleveland mount a comeback in the ALDS.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:43 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians outfielder Jo Adell had a big night in his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, going 2-for-4 with a walk and three RBI. With the game tied 1-1 in the third inning, Adell put the Guardians ahead for good with a three-run triple off of White Sox left-hander Hagen Smith. Across 660 regular-season plate appearances split between the Guardians and the Los Angeles Angels, Adell hit .240/.298/.401 with 23 home runs, 94 RBI, 70 runs scored, and five stolen bases. He was better with Cleveland than he was with Los Angeles, posting a .740 OPS across 204 trips to the plate after the Guardians acquired him at the trade deadline. Adell has notched a couple of key hits for Cleveland in the ALDS and now has four RBI across the first three games of the series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:32 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages had the key hit in his team's 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday, logging a go-ahead two-run single off Braves right-hander Robert Suarez in the seventh inning. Pages finished the game with two hits and two RBI in three at-bats. The 25-year-old was a critical piece of the Dodgers lineup during the regular season, hitting .274 with 23 home runs, 85 RBI, 75 runs scored, and 13 stolen bases. However, Pages struggled mightily during the Dodgers' run to the 2025 World Series, notching just four hits in 55 postseason plate appearances. After his big night on Wednesday, Pages has already logged four hits in just 15 plate appearances in the 2026 playoffs.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:19 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians right-hander Cade Smith was lights out to secure his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Smith entered the game in the eighth inning and recorded the final six outs, logging five strikeouts without allowing a single baserunner. The 27-year-old was one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, pitching to a 1.95 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 107 strikeouts and 41 saves across 74 innings (69 games). Smith has been dominant so far in the Division Series as well, as he's yet to allow a hit or a walk in his four innings of work. If Cleveland is going to mount a comeback in the series, it will likely need Smith to continue his dominance.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:11 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians third baseman Jose Ramirez was one of the stars of his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series. In five plate appearances, Ramirez recorded a double, a triple, a walk, two RBI, two runs scored, and a stolen base. With Cleveland leading 5-3 in the 8th inning, it was Ramirez's two-run triple that sealed the win for the Guardians and kept the series alive to see Game 4. The 34-year-old battled through injuries and underperformance in 2026, hitting .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs, 53 RBI, 71 runs scored, and 37 stolen bases across 544 plate appearances. Ramirez also got off to a slow start in the postseason, going hitless in his first eight trips to the plate against the White Sox. If Cleveland is going to rally all the way back from two games down in the ALDS, it will need Ramirez to stay hot in Games 4 and 5.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Robert Gasser Starting Game 4 of NLDS Against Padres


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:08 PM ET
Milwaukee Brewers left-hander Robert Gasser will start for the Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday night at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres, according to Brewers reporter Sophia Minnaert. It will be Gasser's first career postseason start after throwing 2 2/3 innings of relief in the playoffs for the Brew Crew last year. The 27-year-old southpaw went 5-5 on the season with a 3.87 ERA (4.24 FIP) and 1.19 WHIP with a career-high 103 strikeouts and 35 walks in 109 1/3 innings across 21 appearances (20 starts). The problem for Gasser is that he has not made a start in almost two weeks, so he could be a bit rusty. Manager Pat Murphy will surely have a short hook on the young left-hander as the Brewers look to close the best-of-five series out in San Diego. Gasser was outstanding down the stretch in 2026, allowing two earned runs or fewer in each of his last six starts, walking 12 and striking out 31 in 32 1/3 innings during that span. He did not face the Padres at all during the regular season, which could give him a bit of an advantage.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Sophia Minnaert
Mason Miller Back From the Paternity List for Game 4


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:03 PM ET
The San Diego Padres announced on Wednesday that they returned right-handed closer Mason Miller from the paternity list, taking the place on the National League Division Series roster of left-handed reliever Wandy Peralta. Miller blew a two-inning save in Game 2 of the series in Milwaukee against the Brewers and was then unavailable for the win in Game 3 at Petco Park on Tuesday night. It is great news for the Padres, who did not have left-handed high-leverage reliever Adrian Morejon on Tuesday due to a left-shoulder issue. The Padres had to go to Game 1 starter, right-hander Michael King, for the two-inning save with both Miller and Morejon unavailable. It is uncertain if Morejon will be able to pitch late in the game in another must-win contest on Wednesday in Game 4, but the Padres will at least have their stud closer back in the fold. The two-time All-Star was lights-out during the regular season, his first full season with the Friars, posting a 1.67 ERA (1.17 FIP), 0.900 WHIP, a career-high and league-high 38 saves, a career-high 129 strikeouts, and 26 walks in just 70 innings pitched. With their season on the line, expect manager Craig Stammen to be aggressive in his usage of Miller if Game 4 is close in the later innings, even though he showed command issues in the ninth on Sunday in Milwaukee.--Keith Hernandez
Source: San Diego Padres
Miguel Rojas Not Worried About Back/Hip Injury


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 12:28 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran infielder Miguel Rojas (back, hip) said he felt some tightness in his left lower-back/hip area during a swing in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday against the hosting Atlanta Braves before he was pulled mid at-bat, according to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic. However, Rojas was not concerned about his availability for the rest of the series and going forward. Rojas probably will not be in the Dodgers' starting lineup for Game 4 of the series on Wednesday at Truist Park against Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle, but it sounds like he should be available off the bench. The 37-year-old Venezuelan infielder has made two starts so far in the NLDS against the Braves and has gone 1-for-4 with a double and a strikeout. He was hitless in three at-bats with a strikeout in Tuesday's Game 3 win before being replaced at second base by Tommy Edman. Rojas has mostly been a bench player for the Dodgers in his 13th year in the league (fourth with L.A.) in 2026, but he proved in last year's World Series that he is still capable of coming through in the clutch when needed. He hit .267 (60-for-225) with four homers and 23 RBI during the regular season.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Fabian Ardaya
Oct 7, 2026, 11:57 AM ET
St. Louis Cardinals right-handed closer Riley O'Brien was a first-time All-Star in 2026 in his first full season as the team's closer, and he ended the year tied with San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller for the National League lead in saves (38) with a 4.08 ERA across a career-high 64 innings pitched. O'Brien also set a career high in appearances (66) in his first full year as a big-leaguer. He did not allow an earned run in his first 13 appearances of the year and ended the first half with a 3.43 ERA and a 7.9% walk rate in 39 1/3 frames. O'Brien had 24 saves in his first 28 opportunities. But in 27 appearances after the All-Star break, O'Brien had a 5.11 ERA in 24 2/3 innings, and his walk rate rose to 14.4% while he went 14-for-18 in save chances. Three of his blown saves in the second half came in September, and five of his losing decisions came in his final 13 outings. The 31-year-old said he experienced "fatigue" in the closing days of the season and that his legs have "been feeling heavy compared to how they felt early in the year," according to Daniel Guerrero of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. As he tired, the velocity of O'Brien's pitches suffered. To be able to maintain velocity through the entire season, O'Brien said he plans to focus on putting on "as much muscle as I can."--Keith Hernandez
Source: St. Louis Post-Dispatch - Daniel Guerrero
Curtis Mead the Favorite to Start at Second Base Next Year


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:47 AM ET
Boston Red Sox infielder Curtis Mead is considered the favorite to open next season as the team's starting second baseman, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline this summer, but he ended up playing in only one game for Boston due to a fractured wrist that he suffered in his second at-bat with the team. The 25-year-old will now have all offseason to heal up, and he will enter spring training as the team's primary option at the keystone as they attempt to get back to the playoffs in 2027. The Australian native was having a breakout 2026 campaign with the Nationals before being traded to Boston, and he finished the year with a .253/.353/.498 slash line with an .851 OPS, 17 home runs, 48 RBI, 49 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 285 at-bats in 88 combined games with Washington and Boston. "That would be, I would say, broadly our plan," said manager Chad Tracy when asked about second base. "He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that."--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Walker Buehler to Start Game 4 of NLDS Against Brewers


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:36 AM ET
The San Diego Padres announced that veteran right-hander Walker Buehler will make the start in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday night at Petco Park against the visiting Milwaukee Brewers. Buehler will make his first postseason appearance this year after going 9-6 with a 4.63 ERA (4.51 FIP) and 1.35 WHIP with 131 strikeouts and 57 walks in 153 2/3 innings pitched across his 32 starts for the Padres in his first season with the team. The 32-year-old is no longer the high-end ace that he was with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he does have plenty of postseason experience, posting a 3.04 ERA (3.21 FIP) with 114 strikeouts and 36 walks in 94 2/3 innings pitched. Buehler's last start came on Sept. 26 against the division-rival Arizona Diamondbacks, when he allowed four runs (three earned) with a walk and three strikeouts in just 3 2/3 innings for a no-decision. He picked up a win in his only outing against Milwaukee in 2026, giving up just one earned run with two walks and five strikeouts in six innings at Petco Park back on Aug. 11. Buehler will most definitely be on a short leash in a must-win game for San Diego if he is not on his game early on.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Padres PR
Adrian Morejon Dealing With "Stickiness in his Shoulder"


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
San Diego Padres left-handed reliever Adrian Morejon (shoulder) was unavailable in Game 3 of the National League Division Series at Petco Park on Tuesday night against the Milwaukee Brewers due to "stickiness in his shoulder," manager Craig Stammen told AJ Cassavell of MLB.com. There is still a chance that Morejon will be available for Game 4 against the Brewers in San Diego on Wednesday night as the Friars attempt to force a Game 5 back in Milwaukee on Friday night. With Morejon unavailable and closer Mason Miller on the paternity list, the Padres' bullpen was very short on Tuesday night, but Game 1 starter Michael King came to the rescue and threw the final two innings for SD to pick up a save in the 4-3 victory. Morejon has already had two two-inning appearances in this postseason, once in the Wild-Card Series against the Chicago Cubs and again on Saturday against the Brewers in Game of the NLDS, when he allowed the game-winning home run to catcher William Contreras. The hard-throwing Cuban left-hander was one of the most effective late-inning setup men during the regular season, though, going 9-3 with a 2.83 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, three saves, and a career-high 107 strikeouts in just 86 innings out of the bullpen. With Miller unlikely to be back with the team on Wednesday, the Padres could really use Morejon's left arm on Wednesday evening.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - AJ Cassavell
Oct 6, 2026, 10:58 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman was one of the stars of his team's 3-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday. Freeman had just one hit in four plate appearances, but it was a solo home run off Braves ace Chris Sale. Freeman put together another strong regular season in 2026, hitting .288/.362/.430 with 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 74 runs scored, and seven stolen bases. The 37-year-old's production tailed off late in the year, as he hit just .184 in September and slugged just one home run across 249 plate appearances after the All-Star break. However, Freeman has looked like his vintage self so far this postseason. Across the first three games of the NLDS, Freeman has logged four hits, two home runs, two RBI, and three runs scored.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 6, 2026, 10:40 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers utility man Enrique Hernandez struck one of the big blows of his team's 3-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday, clubbing a two-run home run off of Braves ace Chris Sale to open the scoring in the fourth inning. It was Hernandez's only hit of the night, but it helped the Dodgers chase Sale out of the game after just five innings of work. Hernandez missed a large chunk of the regular season with an oblique injury and was not particularly effective when healthy, hitting .222 with four home runs across 96 plate appearances. However, the 35-year-old has a long history as an unlikely postseason hero. Across 332 career plate appearances in the playoffs, Hernandez has now hit .272 with 18 home runs and 44 RBI.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com

The National League’s top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers head to San Diego, California, with a 2-0 lead in their NLDS matchup against the Padres for Game 3 Tuesday night at Petco Park. The Brewers have a chance to advance to the NLCS for the second consecutive year with a win, while the Padres will be fighting to keep their season alive with the help of their home crowd.
The Brewers earned a first-round bye as the No. 1 seed in the NL and home-field advantage throughout the MLB playoffs after finishing the regular season with the best record in the league. While that extra time off during the Wild Card Series has hurt teams with a first-round bye plenty of times in the past, it hasn’t slowed down Milwaukee, which won the first two games of the NLDS against San Diego.
Both games have been one-run contests so far, with Brewers catcher William Contreras playing the hero in Game 1 with his go-ahead solo home run in the seventh inning as Milwaukee went on to win 3-2. The Brewers followed that with a dramatic 4-3 victory in Game 2 when 22-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio delivered a walk-off two-RBI single against Padres superstar closer Mason Miller.

One of the New York Yankees prime trade deadline needs was believed to be the catcher position. It seemed like a foregone conclusion that the club would target help behind the plate, as Austin Wells struggled miserably throughout the first half of the season. Brian Cashman seemed to feel otherwise.
Wells rebounded somewhat in the second half, hitting .229/.351/.436 down the stretch. Still, the Yankees might not want to roll into 2026 with Wells, or at least might be wary of counting on him as the primary catcher moving forward. There will be options in free agency, highlighted by Ryan Jeffers, but after him there's Tyler Stephenson and a bunch of questionable options. The bidding for Jeffers could get hot, so New York might turn to the trade market to scratch its itch behind the dish.
That could bring a risky trade partner back into the fold: the Milwaukee Brewers, who could find themselves dangling William Contreras in order to bring back a haul.
Trading the soon-to-be 29-year-old would follow the Brewers' M.O. He'll be entering his final year of team control in 2027, and his last two seasons have been good, but a downgrade from his peak in 2023 through 2024. This season, Contreras hit .270/.341/.417 with 18 homers, which is good production regardless of position, but looks even better in light of the fact that he's a catcher
| William Contreras fWAR by year since becoming a regular |
|---|
| 2023 - 5.8 |
| 2024 - 5.5 |
| 2025 - 3.7 |
| 2026 - 3.0 |
A Yankees-Brewers William Contreras trade would be a Devin Williams type of risk that further ignites Red Sox rivalry
Whether Devin Williams flopped because he was on the decline or because he just didn't want to play in New York is unclear, but Milwaukee has a history of fleecing people in these kinds of trades. Just look at what they did to the Mets with Freddy Peralta for further proof.
There's a real reason to engage the Brewers with caution, even for an offensive force at catcher like Contreras. However, if Brian Cashman made a move for the backstop, he'd be throwing even more gas on the Yankees' never-ending rivalry with the Boston Red Sox.
The Red Sox employ William's older brother, Willson Contreras, so such a move would add a sibling rivalry dynamic to the competition between these long-standing enemies. Willson is fiery player, who has both taken Boston's leadership to task while also threatening to use his no-trade clause if the Red Sox approached him about a trade prior to Boston's turn of fortune ahead of the deadline.
William is an equally passionate player, following in his older brother's footsteps with stirring displays of emotion on the field. Putting the two of them together, on opposite sides of the most heated rivalry in sports, would create a highly combustible situation that could be a lot of fun to watch.
It's all speculation for now. The Brewers have shown no indication that they'd want to trade Contreras, and we'd have to admit that while he'd be an intriguing option, we'd be wary if they actively shopped him. At the same time, if he landed in pinstripes and it worked out, next year's Yankees-Red Sox matchups could be full of fireworks and a lot of fun.

On Tuesday, Milwaukee catcher William Contreras appeared on a podcast with former Braves teammate Ronald Acuna Jr. Contreras told his agent to not speak to him for three weeks once the news broke he was heading to Milwaukee, shared by X (formerly Twitter) user Master Flip.

The Milwaukee Brewers have a certain style of play and they aren't going to stray from it, even in a franchise history-making win.
On Thursday, Milwaukee won its 100th game of the season, which is the first time in franchise history that a club has reached triple digits, and the Brewers clinched the No. 1 seed in the National League playoffs at the same time. It was a big night, to say the least. Still, despite everything on the line, Milwaukee didn't change how it handles things. For example, William Contreras — who has been red-hot recently — was benched in the eighth inning with the score knotted at one for not running out a grounder earlier in the game.
Jackson Chourio pinch-hit for Contreras and after the game, Brewers manager Pat Murphy confirmed the reason for the All-Star backstop being pulled, as transcribed by Brewers broadcaster Dominic Cotroneo of 620 WTMJ.
The Brewers Play The Game The Right Way
"He didn't run the ball out and [Trea Turner] muffed it," Cotroneo wrote. "I didn't know whether he was gonna be safe. Everyone knows how much William does for our team, how hard he plays, how much he competes. ... But we don't accept that, and he knows that."
The Brewers play the game the right way, and this is yet another example of how. With win No. 100 and the No. 1 seed in the National League on the line, Milwaukee stuck with the precedent it has had all season. Back in August, Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt was benched in a game for the same thing. He didn't run hard out of the box on a ball that dropped in and got a single, rather than a double.
In Contreras' case, he has been one of the hottest hitters in Milwaukee's lineup recently. Since Aug. 27, he has been slashing .282/.354/.565 with a .918 OPS, six home runs, 28 RBIs, 11 walks, and six doubles. He has been elite and is a big reason why the Brewers were in the position they were in to clinch. That's why it's even more important that the Brewers handled the situation the same way as with the rookie.
They have set the tone and whether you're a multi-time All-Star or a rookie finding your way, in Milwaukee everyone is held to the same standards. It's a good practice to have in professional sports. Plus, it doesn't hurt that Chourio came in and walked, stole a base and then eventually blasted his 25th homer of the season. That makes the decision look a little better, to say the least. The Brewers play the game the right way and were rewarded for it.

item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- Even on the night his team became the first in the Majors in three years to win 100 games, Brewers manager Pat Murphy showed he still has the pedal to the metal.
Murphy pulled one of his best players, All-Star catcher William Contreras, for a pinch-hitter in the eighth inning of Milwaukee’s 5-1 win over the Phillies on Thursday night at Citizens Bank Park. It proved to be the right move, because pinch-hitter Jackson Chourio responded by working a walk, stealing second base and scoring the go-ahead run.
But it was also Murphy sending a message. Contreras had not run hard on a groundout to shortstop Trea Turner in the fifth inning. Turner bobbled the baseball, but still had plenty of time to throw to first for the inning-ending out in a tie game.
“I don’t know if he could have been safe or not,” Murphy said. “Everybody knows how much William does for our team, how hard he plays and how much he competes. But he’s also a guy that people expect a lot out of. We don’t accept that. He knows that.”
It’s not uncommon for Contreras to pick his moments to run hard, and the Brewers generally don’t mind that he does. He’s played at least 141 games and started at least 108 games behind the plate in each of his four seasons with the Brewers, and is the first catcher in Brewers history to catch at least 1,000 innings in three straight seasons. His 1,074 2/3 innings behind the plate this season are most in the Majors.
“There’s never going to be a time when you’re not responsible for playing winning baseball,” Murphy said. “It’s a guy that has done so much for the Brewers, he still has to abide by all the same [rules]. He doesn’t have to go 100 percent every time down the baseline, but when a guy muffs it, you have to be going hard enough that you’re safe if he does muff it.
“That’s winning baseball. Because that at-bat is important. Because every one of those at-bats is important.”
How did Murphy’s move land in the clubhouse?
“I think it’s great. I’m sure you guys have heard him say it because he says it to us all the time: ‘You can’t coast uphill,’” said first baseman Jake Bauers, who supplied Thursday night’s winning hit. “He wants [us] to keep [our] foot on the gas. We want to keep the foot on the gas. And we don’t want to go into the postseason feeling like we already did something. It’s really just, keep our heads down, keep working, keep preparing and go out and execute at a high clip.”
To be fair, Contreras was not the only player who raised Murphy’s ire. Yes, the Brewers won their 100th game in a season for the first time in club history. Yes, they completed a 7-2 final road trip in which they won every series and clinched the division, the best record in franchise history and a first-round bye in the postseason.
But a manager always sees ways his team can be better.
“Out of the 30 teams, very few over the next 10 years will win 100,” Murphy said. “I’m just grateful and proud to be a part of it, truly. And I’m proud we have this group of guys. Now, did we play great baseball tonight? No. Have we been playing great baseball? No. The strikeouts are concerning offensively.
“But, the guys, they like being together and they like this winning thing. They can’t take it for granted, because it’s special. But you have to put in the work to do it.”

The Milwaukee Brewers have a 100-win season. With a victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on Thursday night, the 2026 Brew Crew improved to 100-59 on the 2026 season, reaching an unbelievable milestone that hadn't been accomplished in the first 57 seasons of the franchise's history.
After projection models expected the Brewers to finish with somewhere between 80-85 wins during the 2026 season, Pat Murphy's squad has proved the preseason predictions wrong once again. However, they didn't just surpass their expected win total by a few games; they blew past the projections, produced the best regular season in franchise history, and reached the elusive 100-win mark.
It's an unbelievable accomplishment, one that is made even more impressive by the fact that Milwaukee has produced 90+ win seasons in each of the last four seasons and five times in the last six years. This isn't a one-off season in which the Brewers sacrificed their future and went "all in" on one year. Rather, it's just another chapter in what has easily been the most successful stretch of seasons in franchise history. Put another way, to win 100 games with the best farm system in baseball makes the achievement that much more incredible.
It took a pair of wins over the Philadelphia Phillies, who still have plenty to play for, to achieve 100 wins before their final series of the regular season. With the Brewers fully in postseason preparation mode, made clear by a number of roster and in-game decisions, Murphy's team displayed their impressive depth in their late-September series victory over the Phillies. Said roster depth will be key in the postseason.
Brewers' rely on impressive roster depth to reach elusive 100-win mark after postseason preparation has begun
The Brewers entered Thursday night's series finale against the Phillies with a first-round bye, and therefore a spot in the NLDS, already secured. They didn't have nearly as much to play for as Philadelphia, who is fighting to secure home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series. As a result, Murphy turned to Shane Drohan, who is expected to be a reliever in October, for a short start, didn't include Christian Yelich or Jackson Chourio in the starting lineup, and opted to have William Contreras DH during the series finale on Thursday night. Murphy didn't use Abner Uribe or Trevor Megill and kept Antonio Senzatela in for a save in the ninth inning, and yet, even with their postseason preparation fully underway, the Brewers knocked off the mighty Phillies, who have not officially clinched a spot in the postseason just yet.
In other words, the Brewers won their 100th game of the season on Thursday night due to their impressive roster depth. Murphy's squad proved that they can defeat a postseason team like the Phillies without using one of their top starters, without starting Chourio or Yelich, and without turning to their elite high-leverage duo at the end of the ballgame.
That type of roster depth bodes well for Milwaukee's chances in October. A deep postseason run, like the one the Brewers are hoping to put together, requires contributions throughout the roster. Whether it be a pinch-hit appearance, escaping a jam in the middle innings, or serving as a defensive replacement late in the game, the 26 Brewers that Milwaukee elects to include on their postseason roster will each have their role. It's therefore encouraging to see so many of them contribute to the Brewers' late-season series win over the Phillies, which led to 100 wins.
The Brewers have three games left to improve their record-breaking regular season record even further. Expect a similar strategy, in which Murphy relies on his depth to give necessary rest to each of his players, in the Brewers' upcoming weekend series against the St. Louis Cardinals. That said, regardless of how the final series plays out, the 2026 Brewers officially have a 100-win season to their name -- a truly incredible accomplishment.

Brewers take down Phillies for franchise's first 100-win season
(Photo credit: Bill Streicher)
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run Thursday for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with their 5-1 win over the hosting Philadelphia Phillies.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5 and added a double, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame. Chourio, who pinch-hit for designated hitter William Contreras, led off the frame with a walk off Jose Alvarado (5-4) and stole second.
Gary Sanchez singled deep to left field to put runners on the corners, and after Alvarado got Luis Lara to line out to shallow center, Cooper Pratt (2-for-3) welcomed Chase Shugart with another hit up the middle to give the Brewers a two-run lead. Joey Ortiz added a two-out hit, a blooper to shallow center that allowed Sanchez to score from second.
Chourio added a solo home run, his 25th blast of the season, in the ninth.
Five Brewers pitchers held the Phillies (87-72) to just four hits. JoJo Romero (3-3) allowed one hit in 1 1/3 innings against St. Louis, who Milwaukee acquired him from last month. Romero picked up his second win with the Brewers since coming off the injured list (appendectomy) earlier this month.
Antonio Senzatela relieved Romero, allowing a walk over the final 1 2/3 innings to earn his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter held the Brewers to just one run over six innings. The rookie allowed five hits and three walks while matching a season-high eight strikeouts. His only blemish came in the second, when Sal Frelick doubled home Sanchez.
Kyle Schwarber (2-for-4) and Bryce Harper (2-for-4) combined to get all four of the Phillies hits. Harper's third-inning single scored Schwarber, who led off the frame with a double off Brewers starter Shane Drohan. Philadelphia managed just one hit, a Schwarber single in the seventh, against the Brewers bullpen.
Besides losing the game, the Phillies may also have lost infielder Luis Arraez, who reportedly sprained an ankle trying to avoid a tag on a groundout in the sixth inning.
With the win, Milwaukee can officially clinch home-field advantage throughout the postseason should the Los Angeles Dodgers lose Thursday night to the visiting San Diego Padres.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.
--Field Level Media

Inside Miz's Rise: How Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski Became MLB’s Most Unhittable Starter
This week, Brewers flamethrower and National League Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski will conclude one of the most overpowering, unhittable seasons ever recorded by a starting pitcher.
No qualified starter in modern baseball history has ever surrendered a lower opponent’s batting average than what Misiorowski is allowing now (.159). Take away the shortened 2020 season, and only one starter — Gerrit Cole in 2019 — has ever generated a higher strikeout rate over the course of a full season than Misiorowski’s 38.2% mark this year.
So, it might seem strange that MLB’s velocity king — whose triple-digit heat has reached as high as 105.5 mph, the fastest ever recorded by a starting pitcher — grew up idolizing a pitcher whose average career four-seam velocity clocked in around 90 mph.
Adam Wainwright, who can count on one hand how many big leaguers have ever told him he was one of their favorite players, was taken aback when I told him that he was Misiorowski’s childhood idol.
"He might’ve gotten the first 92, 93 mph from me," Wainwright quipped. "The other 12 are on him."
As of a month ago, Misiorowski had never met or talked to Wainwright. But as a kid in the Kansas City area with little winning baseball to watch in the early 2000s, Misiorowski was drawn to the St. Louis right-hander — not because Wainwright overwhelmed his competition with sheer force, the way Misiorowski can do, but because he was unflappable.
"The biggest thing was his demeanor on the mound," Misiorowski told me last month. "Something bad happens, move onto the next pitch. There’s no care, no emotion with it. I took that into just pitching in general. Whenever I give up a home run or something like that, ‘OK, so be it, they got to me, next pitch.’"
That, admittedly, was not always so easy for Misiorowski.
(Getty Images)
"They used to tear me up, and I’d get really upset on the mound," Misiorowski said. "Then I started watching other guys. I kind of thought about Wainwright and his demeanor and just everyone in the past and kind of was like, ‘That’s what I need to do. I need to forget about it.’"
Along with harnessing his control, adding to his powerful arsenal and maturing into his 6-foot-7-inch frame, Misiorowski’s mental growth on the mound is part of the transformation that has helped the raw prospect with elite tools develop into MLB’s most dominant starter over the course of just one year.
The best pitcher on the best team in baseball leads MLB in ERA, WHIP, strikeouts, strikeout rate and opponents’ batting average, among a litany of categories.
"Emotionally, he’s in a way better place," Brewers manager Pat Murphy told me. "I always say, your first year you’re on rollerskates. You don’t feel the concrete on the ground. It’s a little slippery. I feel like he’s taken off the rollerskates. He’s not all the way there. He’s not all the way matured. He’s going to face more adversity. But he’s handled what adversity has come his way pretty darn well."
‘Unlike Anything You Ever See’
Despite his junior college background, Misiorowski’s stuff was never a question.
The velocity that "Miz" generated from his long levers was enough to convince the Brewers to spend a second-round pick in 2022 on the gangly right-hander from Crowder College, who would otherwise have been transferring to LSU for his junior season.
(Photo by Tim Nwachukwu/Getty Images)
In his first full pro season in Milwaukee’s system in 2023, Misiorowski jumped from Low-A to High-A to Double-A, combining to strike out 110 batters in 71.1 innings. Days before Misiorowski’s first Double-A start against the Montgomery Biscuits, his pitching coach, Will Schierholz, saw him throw in person for the first time. The first pitch of the bullpen session clocked in at 98 mph. Then Misiorowski spun a slider at 92.
"We had some pretty good arms, some major league arms, on that staff, and you’re awestruck when you watch Miz throw up close for the first time," Schierholz, who’s now a Brewers assistant pitching coordinator, told me. "It’s unlike anything you ever see."
In Misiorowski’s last three starts that season, he struck out 29 batters in just 14.2 innings. He’d spike curveballs into the dirt, and opponents would still chase. He’d fire fastballs three feet above the zone, and hitters would still helplessly offer. Many times, they were simply guessing as soon as the ball left his hand.
"Every time he touched the mound, he knew hitters did not have a chance," Schierholz said. "If he made his pitch, they didn’t have a chance."
The problem, however, was that Misiorowski often didn’t know where the ball was going. In five starts at Double-A that season, Misiorowski walked 16 batters and hit 11.
"He was always ultra, ultra competitive, it just wasn’t always a consistent mindset on the mound when things maybe didn’t go his way," Schierholz recalled. "So to see kind of where that’s gone over the last couple years here, to see him have that consistent mindset, calm and collected at all times, that’s come a long way since he came up to Biloxi in 2023."
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
As the strikeouts continued to rack up a year later, so did the free passes. Over 79.2 innings at Double-A in 2024, Misiorowski struck out 105 batters, walked 50 and plunked 10.
When he was promoted to Triple-A that August, the Brewers put him in the bullpen, in part to limit his innings. He clearly had a big-league arm, but his lack of control threatened to make him a reliever long-term.
"I think that was always in the back of everybody’s head, right?" Schierholz said. "Especially for a guy with that prolific stuff. Just in general, you don’t see starters have the stuff that he has. But I think the thing that always kept all of us optimistic is the arsenal’s deep. He didn’t have a big injury history, and he was still so young that we had time to make sure this played out in a positive way."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Misiorowski returned to starting at the beginning of the 2025 season at Triple-A. The control issues lingered, which was part of the reason he was MLB’s No. 68 overall prospect that year and not a top-10 talent. Over a five-start stretch, he struck out 38 batters in 30.2 innings with a 0.79 ERA. But then came four starts in which he combined for 12 walks over 14 innings.
Still, despite Misiorowski’s volatility, depth issues in the Brewers’ big-league rotation spurred action. They called up the 23-year-old, who did not look overwhelmed by the promotion.
After just five MLB starts, the last of which was a six-inning, 12-strikeout gem against Clayton Kershaw and the reigning champion Dodgers, Misiorowski was named an All-Star. Some scoffed at MLB’s decision, but he looked deserving of the honor when he threw a scoreless eighth inning in an eventual National League win.
"He’s taken the game straight out of the firehose," Brewers pitching coach Chris Hook told me. "It was a lot. I thought he did an incredible job for as much as was thrown at him."
But adversity beckoned, as it does so often for rookies.
An Early Turning Point
Opponents went from hitting .138 against Misiorowski in the first half to .257 in the second half. Lefties feasted on his slider, his strikeout rate declined, his control and command remained spotty, and the Brewers wanted to be cautious of his workload, considering he had never thrown even 100 innings in a professional season.
Hook sensed Misiorowski was wearing down, both physically and mentally.
"The intensity here is higher, and then you’re pitching more often," Hook explained. "At the end of September, he felt it. It was a lot of strain."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
After Misiorowski registered a 5.45 ERA in nine starts out of the break, he was moved to the bullpen at the end of the season. He didn’t like the way he was handling himself or how he handled getting hit around.
So, he thought back to Wainwright. About the mindset. About letting go.
Then, he rose to the occasion with the lights at their brightest.
In a bulk relief role, Misiorowski recorded a 1.50 ERA over 12 playoff innings. His postseason ended with five innings of one-run ball at Dodger Stadium, where he struck out nine batters in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series. It wasn’t enough to lift his Brewers over the eventual back-to-back champs, but he looked at that moment as a turning point in his career.
"I went through the struggles at the end of the year, and really was trying to battle through it," Misiorowski said. "Then, postseason rolled around, had the success, and I kind of brought it into this year, still on that momentum."
He demonstrated his ability to control his emotions on baseball’s biggest stage.
Then he focused on everything else within his control — his body, his arsenal, the strike zone — to ascend into a starting pitching marvel.
"When you fail, and you’ve been one of the best pitchers on the planet and quickly one of the youngest All-Stars of all time, I’m sure that can take a toll on anybody," Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told me. "But he’s a mature kid. He’s grown up to be a man right in front of us, and he’s a guy that you want at the front of any rotation. He’s the best pitcher in the game, in my opinion."
Controlling His Body
Over the offseason, Misiorowski went to work on building his slender frame, knowing he needed more force and stamina to hold up over the long haul of a season after last year’s dropoff.
"It was definitely more lower-body focused," he told me. "I wanted to get my legs as strong as possible. That’s where most of my power comes from."
He ended last year around 185 pounds. Crossing the 200-pound mark this winter was a milestone moment. He didn’t stop. He said he came into camp at around 215-220 pounds and is now around 210-215, a 30-pound increase from last year.
He didn’t change his diet entirely, but he acknowledged there were fewer 3 a.m. visits to Taco Bell with his friends.
"Eating well, eating better," Misiorowski explained, "not crappy, like I was. Really working on finally maturing into my body."
Where does he see the weight helping most now?
"The biggest is definitely stamina," he said. "The effort isn’t max effort every time. You can still get to the 100s, and it’s an easier effort compared to last year when I was hitting 100 and it was full go."
Of all the improvements Misiorowski has made, it’s the velocity jump that stands out most to Schierholz, his old minor-league pitching coach. What Misiorowski is doing is unmatched and unprecedented.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
Prior to this season, the fastest average four-seamer for a qualified MLB starter over the course of a full season belonged to Noah Syndergaard at 98.9 mph in 2016. Misiorowski is averaging 100.6 mph this year, up more than a tick from a season ago.
There have been 365 occasions of a starting pitcher crossing the 102-mph mark this season. The Pirates’ Bubba Chandler did it twice. So did Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez, when he was used as an opener. The other 361 times are courtesy of Misiorowski, who has also eclipsed 103 mph 143 times, 104 mph 22 times and 105 mph once.
A year ago, he threw just 22 pitches over 102 mph, including the postseason.
"I think we try to lay out plans for the guys, but all the credit goes to him, the work that he put in," Arnold said. "You gotta want to be great, and I think Miz is exactly that kind of kid. He knew what he needed to do to get better, and he did it himself."
And now, Misiorowski has a better idea of where his four-seamer is going — even if he’s not entirely sure why.
Controlling The Zone
Misiorowski’s fastball gets the highlights and acclaim, but arguably the most dramatic and important change Misiorowski made this year has nothing to do with his power.
He has cut his walk rate down from 11% last year to 6.6% this year, the largest year-to-year drop among all qualified MLB starters.
But he can’t explain how.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
"I honestly have no clue," Misiorowski told me. "I wish I could tell you and help everyone out. I honestly have zero idea on how I’m doing it. It’s one of those things I’m looking at like, ‘That number ain’t right.’"
Many of his teammates assumed he must be pounding the strike zone a lot more, but he’s actually in the zone less this year than he was last season.
That might seem confusing, but his pitching coach has an explanation.
"You can’t wait him out," Hook said. "He’s throwing 105 [mph], and it’s like, ‘I gotta go if he’s throwing a strike.’"
"It’s going to be hard to put the ball in play," Arnold added, "so teams are probably wanting to be aggressive and see if they can hop on something."
It helps that Misiorowski is throwing a first-pitch strike 8% more this year than last year — also the largest year-to-year jump from any qualified starter this season.
And it plays into Brewers closer Trevor Megill’s theory.
"You make one pitch a strike on the corner, then the one off the corner by three inches looks like it’s closer than it is," Megill told me.
Misiorowski’s chase rate (35.2%) is up nearly 7% from last season.
Meanwhile, his whiff rate (37.2%) is the highest among all qualified starters and is also up significantly from a year ago (29.7%) — again, that’s the biggest year-to-year jump for a starting pitcher in MLB.
Misiorowski’s enhanced ability to harness his stuff has led to shorter innings, longer outings and even a game between him and his pitching coach.
One time earlier this year, Misiorowski was coming off a 12-pitch frame when Hook issued a test.
"I said, ‘Hey, can you make it a 10 next?’ He made it a 10,’" Hook recalled. "I said, ‘Can you make it a nine?’ We just like having those challenges inside the game."
Controlling His Arsenal
Earlier this year, Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn watched Misiorowski’s fastball up close and followed up with a question.
Why the hell are you throwing anything else?
"It was funny," Misiorowski recalled. "But on the flipside, I’m like, ‘I can’t just do that.’"
In some ways, though, Misiorowski has heeded Wynn’s advice.
His four-seam usage is up this year, and no starter in baseball throws their heater more. With a fastball that averages over 100 mph and is responsible for 163 of his MLB-leading 247 strikeouts, you can understand why.
At the same time, Misiorowski is still adding to his repertoire.
"It seems to me like he went home and said, ‘You know what, the postseason was fun, I want to get back there again, how can I be a great pitcher and not just a thrower?’" Wainwright said. "That is the nature of how great players mature. That’s the nature of how great players grow in the game. They don’t get comfortable in who they are. They don’t get stuck."
Last year, lefties hit .385 and righties hit .267 against Misiorowski’s slider, which averaged 5 mph slower than his four-seamer. The Brewers wanted to find another offering that would create more of a separation in velocity.
So, Misiorowski added a slower slider with more depth to his arsenal this year, which righties are hitting .188 against. Meanwhile, he turned last year’s slider into his cutter, which lefties are hitting .089 against this season.
"I’ve gotten a lot of strange looks, strange emotions, from it, just in the fact that the cutter’s kind of closer to the heater," Misiorowski said. "You get some swings where some guys see the spin, and then they’re like, ‘Oh, shoot, it’s on me.’"
(Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
In addition to his curveball and changeup, the new additions to his arsenal give opponents more to think about this season beyond his velocity.
"He kind of does things on the fly a little bit," Hook said. "I’m not saying he’s a lab kid, per se. He’s naturally gifted, and he’s like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ ‘I can do that,’ and he makes the adjustment."
Along with a lower walk rate, Misiorowski’s strikeout rate is up 6.2% from last season and is the highest in MLB. He won’t win the triple crown — Phillies ace Cristopher Sánchez has three more wins than him — but he leads the sport in both ERA and strikeouts, despite ranking 23rd in innings pitched.
His triple-digit heat combined with better control and command certainly help, but so does the tweak in his repertoire. He’s also gaining a better feel for game-planning and why his catchers are calling for certain pitches in certain situations.
"At the start of the year, we were definitely more, ‘Whatever you think, let’s just roll with it. You’re obviously seeing something that’s working,’" Misiorowski told me. "And it’s gotten to the point where it’s like, ‘OK, I’m kinda seeing it too. I understand where you’re going with this."
‘This Guy Is Built For This’
More often than not, though, he relies on his catchers to help him navigate a game, as William Contreras did during his 15-strikeout, one-hit, complete-game shutout on 95 pitches against the Phillies in June.
Contreras also helped Misiorowski work around trouble two months later, when the pitcher made his return to the mound at Dodger Stadium for the first time since the NLCS.
(Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)
A year ago, Misiorowski was stupefied watching Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman sign his jersey at the All-Star Game. In some ways, he’s still that wide-eyed kid, pinching himself about his new reality.
"I don’t think that will ever get to a point where it’s just normal," Misiorowski told me.
Only now, he’s starting to gain the poise of the idols he grew up watching.
The day before his start on Aug. 15, Misiorowski’s newfound confidence was on full display when he gave away his attack plan against Ohtani.
"He knows what I’m going to do: I’m going to throw a heater," Misiorowski vowed. "Good luck. Here it is."
Sure enough, he followed up on those words by attacking Ohtani with six straight fastballs in his first at-bat, all over 102 mph, to induce a popout. But it’s what Misiorowski did in his final at-bat against Ohtani that exemplified why he is so much more than the novice flamethrower he was a year ago.
After three straight singles off Misiorowski in the fifth inning, Ohtani stepped to the plate with the bases loaded and one out. This time, at Contreras’ behest, Misiorowski switched it up. He got a swinging strike on a curveball, a called strike on a four-seamer, then sent Ohtani back to the dugout swinging through a slider.
"He’s thinking more like a pitcher," Contreras told me, "and not just wanting to throw hard."
(Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images)
One batter later, Misiorowski used the slider again to fool Freddie Freeman on a strikeout and escape the threat. He pumped his fist and let out a scream before returning to the dugout.
As he attempts to follow Wainwright’s lead with his composure on the mound, he’s not losing himself in the process.
"That part of his game hasn’t changed, which I’m happy to see," Schierholz said. "That’s part of what makes him special, is the competitiveness and pitching with emotion, as long as he continues to rein it in and keep it in control."
The Brewers are counting on that as they rumble toward the best record in baseball for a second straight season, this time hoping their Cy Young favorite can help them author a new ending to their franchise’s winningest chapter.
"Obviously, it’s a different animal when you get into October," Misiorowski said. "But it’s going to be exciting, and I think we have a team that can make a run at it."
"This guy," Hook added, "is built for this."

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia’s potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night.
The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next season and are coming off consecutive NL East titles.
The Phillies have to settle for a wild-card berth this season and are likely to open the playoffs next week on the road. The Phillies, Chicago and San Diego hold the three NL wild cards headed into the final games of the season.
The Phillies went 0 for 12 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers and left 10 runners on base.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said ahead of the game the team was willing to wait at Citizens Bank Park until after the Padres game ended, if necessary, to celebrate. No need to hang around.
Aaron Nola (7-11) had turned around a miserable season and posted a 1.86 ERA over his last eight starts as the longest-tenured Phillie got the chance to clinch. With a playoff party looming, he instead surrendered Turang’s 20th homer of the season in the first inning and Yelich’s 12th of the year in the second.
The Phillies scored their only run in the second inning after loading the bases with no outs against Brewers starter Logan Henderson (11-3). Henderson allowed four hits and one run over five innings to help the NL Central champion Brewers win their 99th game of the season.
Trevor Megill worked a scoreless ninth for his 30th save.
William Contreras extended his hitting streak to 11 games with a two-run single in the third for a 4-1 lead.
Nola struck out eight in six innings.
Up next
The Brewers did not announce a starter for Thursday's game. The Phillies send RHP Andrew Painter (3-10, 5.59 ERA) to the mound.

PHILADELPHIA — Zack Wheeler expressed, on one hand, surety Tuesday night. On the other, genuine surprise and gratitude.
Of course, the Phillies right-handed starter went into the game against Milwaukee knowing he was on 1,997 career strikeouts. He understood what it meant that only 95 pitchers in the history of baseball – and nine active – had crossed the 2,000-strikeout threshold.
But at plenty of junctures in a big-league career that started at age 23 but got derailed for two years, he never imagined he’d reach such a round number.
“It’s really cool, special,” Wheeler said after striking out 11 Brewers in a 6-4 Phillies win. “Some of the guys asked me in here, would you ever have thought? The answer is no. Getting into the league, trying to get your feet under you, trying to last, game to game early on, just trying to stay up in the big leagues and trying to figure it out was hard for me. And just being where I am now, it’s pretty special.”
The flipside to that disbelief, though, was the rock-steady assuredness that at age 36, Wheeler could get back to where he was at 35.
On Sept. 22, 2025, Wheeler went to sleep with thoracic decompression surgery scheduled for the next day, the removal of a rib relieving a circulation issue that had led to blood clots and ended his season.
He headed home 365 days later having made his 27th and likely final start of the season, three more than last year despite a delayed start to the season. He carries a 13-5 record, a 3.06 ERA and, by wins above replacement, his third-most valuable season among seven as a Phillie.
Which has to be at least a little surprising, right?
“I would expect it,” Wheeler said when asked if he would’ve been surprised to learn these were his stats a year post-surgery. “You’ve got to have that confidence. That’s all it is. It’s just confidence. It’s not anything else than that. You have to expect to be back to who you were. You’ve got to keep that mindset. If not, then who knows what’s going to go on in your head, and that can translate to you coming back and how you perform.”
How he performed Tuesday was as he has most of the season: Rock solid. He made quick work of the milestone, striking out the side in the first inning. His 310 career games to reach 2,000 strikeouts ties Felix Hernandez for the 13th-fewest in history.
He struck out the side in the second, too. With a whiff of Luis Lara to start the third, he set the Phillies franchise record. Already in his mind was the then-major league mark he watched from the dugout in New York in 2014, when Mets teammate Jacob deGrom fanned the first eight Marlins to tie the modern record set in 1986 by Houston’s Jim Deshaies. (deGrom’s bid was broken up by a single by the pitcher, former Phillies farmhand Jarred Cosart; the MLB record was re-set in 2021 when Miami’s Pablo Lopez struck out the first nine Braves he faced.)
“All I could think about was deGrom doing that when we were down in Miami back in the day, and the pitcher came up and got the bat on the ball,” he said. “So I was just trying to beat him, honestly. Once I got through that second inning, I was like, ‘All right, I’m trying to do this.’”
Wheeler’s run was broken by a groundout to third by Cooper Pratt. He retired the first nine in order before Garrett Mitchell looped a single off the glove of a backtracking Bryson Stott at third to lead off the fourth. Mitchell scored on William Contreras’s sac fly to get the Brewers within 3-1.
A lead-off single by nine-hitter David Hamilton and a walk to Jackson Chourio put two on in the sixth. Wheeler froze Brice Turang, Hamilton and Chourio stealing third and second. Contreras beat Wheeler on a first-pitch fastball that was a little too low, the catcher golfing a liner just over the reach of a leaping Trea Turner at short for a two-run single and a 3-3 game, sending Wheeler to the no-decision.
“I wanted to go in, but it was down. I wanted it more up,” he said. “Down’s a little easier to hit than up. That’s probably what I was most upset about tonight, and probably the pitch I hate the most so far this season.”
There hasn’t been much to regret this year. Wheeler’s injury dealt a huge confidence blow to the Phillies heading into the postseason last year. It started him on the injured list in 2026, but he blew through the six month estimated timeline to debut by the end of April.
From that point on, he was the Zack Wheeler of old, so much so that he’s likely to start the first game of a Phillies Wild Card series despite not being one of the team’s two All-Star starters this season.
A month into his return, his ERA sat at 1.67, excluding a five-start stretch from late July to late August in which he allowed 23 earned runs in 24.1 innings around an rain-interrupted outing in Baltimore, he’s been spectacular, with an ERA of 2.05 over his other 22 starts.
Wheeler isn’t prone to reflection, especially midseason. The strikeout milestone forced a bit of it upon him. He still approached it as having one start left, though he’d only pitch in Sunday’s finale if the Phillies need it, which is highly avoidable at a magic number of 2 after Tuesday’s action.
He took the chance to express gratitude: to his wife and family, to the catchers and coaches he’s had through his 12 major league seasons. He reserved a special mention for Phillies head athletic trainer Paul Buchheit for the rehabilitation plan from last year.
The round number offered perspective, for a blue-chip prospect who was outstanding in his first two seasons more than a decade ago but then missed two full seasons with a complicated recovery from Tommy John surgery. He’s navigated the jump from New York to Philly for two big contracts, weathered changes to the expectations of the position, bridged eras from batting to designated hitters, from pitch clocks to ABS.
Through it all, Wheeler has continually dealt every fifth day, which is what a milestone like Tuesday’s fetes.
“The road was hard coming back from that,” Wheeler said of his Tommy John ordeal. “That was another point where I didn’t know what to expect because it was taking longer than what we all expected at the time. So, I was just trying to get back out there. It was kind of like starting over again, just trying to get back out there, just lasting, and I was able to figure it out.”
